text:
Okay, thanks. I found Q3 relatively straightforward, though thinking about *how* that data would be secured was always at the back of my mind. The questions around sensitive data – nationality, disability, ethnicity – felt particularly weighty and I answered ‘never’ across the board for identification purposes; it feels like a huge ethical line to cross unless there's an overwhelmingly compelling reason.

I think Q4 about explainability is *crucially* important. A system nobody understands won't be trusted. My answer reflecting a preference for at least 'small' improvement with high explainability felt strongly right to me, and I’m glad everyone seemed to agree on that. 

Interestingly, almost everyone was okay with losing some accuracy (Q5.1) to ensure fairness - I wonder if that reflects a broader societal awareness now of algorithmic bias?

Thanks. I agree with S8 about Q3 – security wasn’t *in* the question, but it felt implicit and crucial to consider. The sensitive data questions were hard because “improve identification” feels too vague; improve for *whom*? It's easy to say "never" when that detail isn't specified.

I flagged moderate improvements for first-gen and financial aid status – as an advisor, I see those factors consistently impacting student success. But absolutely no age, gender or ethnicity data should be used for identification. 

Q4 felt vital. As advisors, we *need* to understand why a student is flagged. Q5’s consensus on fairness being worth some accuracy loss is encouraging; it reflects good values, but we need oversight to ensure ‘equal recall’ isn't achieved through harmful means.

Thanks both of you. I agree with S8 about Q3 – security wasn’t explicitly stated, and it needs to be a core consideration. The sensitive data questions were really tough. I went with ‘never’ for most because the risk feels too high, even if there *might* be some benefit. As someone who restarted a degree after dropping out, I know things can feel overwhelming quickly, but that doesn't justify intrusive data collection.

I also think Q4 is vital; explainability builds trust. And yes to S3’s point - “improve identification” needs more context! 

I was glad to see consensus on fairness (Q5), and I flagged 'first-gen' and ‘financial aid’ as potentially useful for identifying support needs, but only if it doesn’t reinforce disadvantage. It felt important to acknowledge those barriers exist without making them part of the *system* that identifies students.

Thanks everyone. I agree with much of what’s been said. Question 3 felt alright, though the lack of detail about data security *was* a nagging concern – it feels like a prerequisite for even considering using any of this data. The sensitive data questions were particularly difficult; as an advisor, I see how those factors impact students, but using them for identification is… unsettling, to say the least.

Q4’s importance can't be overstated. As advisors, we need to *explain* interventions to students – a black box model is useless. I also flagged moderate improvements for first-gen and financial aid status, seeing those often. What struck me was the near-universal agreement on fairness (Q5). That’s encouraging. Perhaps an opt-out mechanism could mitigate concerns around data use even further?

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 quite difficult, actually. As a new international student, I'm already aware my data is being handled differently – visa requirements and so on. Adding more data collection for this model feels…intrusive, even if it’s meant to help. That's why I was strict with the ‘acceptable only if…’ options.

I agree explainability (Q4) is crucial. Coming from a different education system, I need to understand *why* something is happening, not just that it is. 

I answered similarly to many on Q5 – fairness is key. But I think we should be cautious about assuming ‘equal recall’ is always best. Maybe focusing on ensuring access to support for *all* students, regardless of group, would be more effective than trying to perfectly equalize identification rates?

Thanks everyone. I agree with S5 – as a student currently navigating chronic health conditions *and* using disability support services, Q3 felt particularly fraught. The idea of adding more data points, even with safeguards, feels… exposing. I marked 'small' for disability-related information only because the university *already* has that data through my access to support; adding it to a predictive model still makes me uneasy.

I think Q4 is incredibly important – as an advisor pointed out, we need to be able to explain things to students. And Q5’s consensus on fairness is good, but S5’s point about universal access feels right too. Perhaps focusing on strengthening existing support services *before* building a potentially biased predictive model would be a better first step?

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really difficult – especially with my own history of dropping out and being diagnosed with ADHD later on. It feels like a lot of trust to ask students to give up more data, even if it’s meant to help. I marked ‘small’ for disability because the university *already* has that info through my access to support, but still… it feels risky. 

Q4 is vital – transparency is everything. And seeing everyone agree on fairness in Q5 is good. But S5 and S3 both made really important points about universal access *instead of* focusing solely on equal identification rates. Maybe we need to improve what’s already there before building something new, especially given the potential for bias. An opt-out would also be essential for me.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 felt particularly sensitive as an advisor. While data security wasn't *in* the question, it absolutely underpins everything; we have a duty of care here. The sensitive data questions were tough. I marked ‘never’ for most, but allowed 'small' improvements for first-gen and financial aid status – I consistently see these impact student success. 

I strongly agree with the emphasis on explainability (Q4). We *need* to be able to justify interventions to students. And Q5’s focus on fairness is vital. S3 & S5 raised excellent points about universal access being potentially more effective than chasing equal recall, and I think that's a crucial consideration before we build anything new. Perhaps strengthening existing services should be the priority.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 quite stressful, honestly. As an international student who works part-time, my situation already feels… precarious. Adding more data points for a predictive model just increases that feeling of being under scrutiny. While I marked ‘moderate’ for course performance and credits – those feel less invasive – I generally leaned towards needing significant improvement before accepting further data use.

Q4 felt vital; explainability builds trust, especially for someone new to the Danish system. And seeing the consensus on fairness (Q5) is reassuring. But S3 & S5 highlighted a crucial point: perhaps *improving existing support* should be the priority instead of building something potentially biased. I’d feel much safer with that approach. An opt-out would also be essential for me.

Thanks everyone. Q3 really resonated with my experience dropping out and restarting – it’s easy to feel like you're being judged when things are tough. I was stricter on data use than many, marking 'never' for age, gender, race, and disability. It feels too invasive, even knowing the university already *has* some of that information. 

I strongly agree with Q4’s focus on explainability; as someone who had to navigate a new system and language, understanding *why* decisions are made is crucial. And I appreciate S3 & S5 pointing out that improving existing support might be more effective than a complex model. An opt-out would definitely make me feel safer. My notes reflect a preference for caution – help should be offered, but not at the cost of privacy or trust.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really difficult, honestly. Being a first-year student *with* dyslexia already makes me feel like I’m constantly being assessed. Adding more data feels… exposing, even though it's supposedly to help. I marked ‘small’ for disability only because the university already knows about it through my exam access arrangements – but adding that to a model still feels risky.

Q4 is hugely important; explainability builds trust. And I agree with S3 and S5 – strengthening existing support services *before* building something new seems much safer, especially given potential biases. An opt-out would be essential for me too. It’s about feeling supported, not scrutinised.

Okay, thanks everyone. I found Q3 incredibly difficult – especially given my own experiences with a long-term mental health condition and being a bit behind on my thesis. The idea of adding more data feels… exposing, even though it's intended to help. While I marked ‘moderate’ for course performance because it *feels* less invasive, I was strict about sensitive data – 'small' only for nationality and disability as the university already has that information through support services access.

Q4 is crucial; explainability builds trust, especially when you're feeling vulnerable. I strongly agree with S3, S5 & others - let’s strengthen what *already exists* before building something new, and an opt-out would be essential for me to feel safe.
